title: Methodus nova et facilis calculum variationum tractandi

deep.reconstruction:
Context: in E420 Euler re-derives the Euler–Lagrange equation by his new δ-method. For J = ∫Z dx with dZ = M dx + N dy + P dp + Q dq + ... (p = y', q = y'', ...), the extremal satisfies 0 = N − dP/dx + d²Q/dx² − .... On the previous page he observed that this equation is generically of even order (2, 4, 6, ...). He then sorts problems into classes by the order of that equation. Class I is the case where the equation is finite (algebraic), so it has no arbitrary constants.

Top of this page, case Z = Z(x,y) only. The equation is N = ∂Z/∂y = 0, which determines a unique curve with no free constants. Example: J = ∫(2xy − y²) dx. Then N = 2(x − y), so the extremal is y = x, the line at 45° to the axis. Along it the integrand is x², so J = x³/3. Euler states that this value is smaller than for any other curve over the same abscissa.

§49 shows that Class I is not exhausted by this case. Let 𝔷(x,y) be arbitrary with d𝔷 = 𝔐 dx + 𝔑 dy, and put Z = 𝔷 p. Then M = 𝔐p, N = 𝔑p, P = 𝔷. The Euler–Lagrange equation is
0 = 𝔑p − d𝔷/dx = 𝔑p − 𝔐 − 𝔑p = −𝔐,
again a finite equation. Euler explains this directly: since p dx = dy, ∫𝔷 p dx = ∫𝔷 dy, which is the first case with x and y interchanged.

Generalisation: for every functional ∫(Z + 𝔷p) dx = ∫(Z dx + 𝔷 dy), with Z and 𝔷 functions of x and y, the extremal condition is 0 = N − 𝔐, i.e. ∂Z/∂y − ∂𝔷/∂x = 0. In modern terms this is the degenerate (affine-in-velocity) Lagrangian L = A(x,y) + B(x,y)y', whose Euler–Lagrange equation collapses to the algebraic curve A_y − B_x = 0. The next page begins Class II: Z depends genuinely on p, giving a second-order equation and two constants fitted to two endpoints.
errors: Max/min error in the example. Since 2xy − y² = x² − (x − y)², the integrand along any curve is at most x², with equality only on y = x. So y = x gives the MAXIMUM of ∫(2xy − y²) dx, and x³/3 is larger, not smaller ('qui utique minor est'), than the value for any other curve over the same abscissa. Euler's statement has the inequality reversed.
Gap: Euler does not mention the case N − 𝔐 ≡ 0 identically. Then Z dx + 𝔷 dy is exact, the integral is path-independent (a null Lagrangian), and every curve is 'extremal'.
Gap: endpoint conditions are not addressed. The finite curve N = 0 (or N − 𝔐 = 0) generally does not pass through prescribed endpoints, so with fixed endpoints there is no smooth extremal.

Gap: for affine-in-p Lagrangians the curve N − 𝔐 = 0 is generally not an extremum at all. By Green's theorem, ∮(Z dx + 𝔷 dy) = −∬(Z_y − 𝔷_x) dA, so comparison curves on either side of the singular curve give values of both signs of the difference. Euler presents it as 'the' max/min curve without this caveat.

ideas.what: When Z depends only on x and y, the Euler–Lagrange equation reduces to the algebraic condition ∂Z/∂y = 0 (pointwise optimisation), with no arbitrary constants.
ideas.where_published: E65 Methodus inveniendi (1744), discussion of formulae whose Euler equation is finite; repeated here in E420

ideas.what: A Lagrangian linear in y', ∫(Z + 𝔷p) dx, gives the finite equation N − 𝔐 = Z_y − 𝔷_x = 0. Explained by rewriting ∫𝔷 p dx = ∫𝔷 dy and interchanging the coordinates.
ideas.modern_name: Affine-in-velocity (degenerate) Lagrangian; singular arc Z_y − 𝔷_x = 0
ideas.usually_credited_to: Euler for the equation; Miele (1950s) for the Green's-theorem treatment of such problems
ideas.where_published: E65 (1744) treats cases yielding finite equations; E420 restates it

ideas.what: Classification of variational problems by the (even) order of the Euler–Lagrange equation and hence by the number of arbitrary constants, i.e. boundary data.
ideas.modern_name: Order of the Euler–Lagrange equation and well-posed boundary conditions

missed.claim: Euler's worked example asserts that x³/3 is the minimum, whereas it is clearly the maximum, since 2xy − y² = x² − (x − y)². This is a small slip in the text; I am unsure whether the Opera omnia editors flagged it.
missed.quote: pro qua ergo valor formulae propositae integralis est x³/3, qui vtique minor est, quam si vlla alia linea curua sumeretur
missed.why_it_might_matter_today: Only for editorial accuracy of the text; no mathematical consequence.

missed.claim: Euler isolates exactly the class ∫(Z dx + 𝔷 dy) whose extremal condition is the curl-type curve ∂Z/∂y − ∂𝔷/∂x = 0. He does not link this to the Green/Stokes area-integral argument (Miele's method in 20th-century trajectory optimisation), which shows such curves are usually not true extrema. This connection is well known in modern control theory, so it is not new.
missed.quote: omnes formulas integrales huiusmodi ∫(Z + 𝔷p)dx ... aequatio ... 0 = N − 𝔐
missed.why_it_might_matter_today: Historically, an early explicit appearance of singular-arc problems linear in the control. No new mathematics.

deep.surprise_reason: The page contains standard material: degenerate Euler–Lagrange equations, already in Methodus inveniendi. The only notable item is an apparent max/min slip in the example.
transcription_corrections: Transcription matches the image well. The fraction after 'integralis est' is x³/3 (printed small), as transcribed.
In the displayed equation, the last term reads −𝔐 (Fraktur M); the transcription is correct.
